headline: Paraguay removes its president after a bank fails

sources.title: Ousted Paraguay president under house arrest after banking crisis leaves 60% of country unable to access accounts (The Guardian)
Paraguay's Santiago Pena under arrest, new president Pedro Alliana sworn in (Al Jazeera)
Paraguay resumes Pena impeachment proceedings as financial crisis deepens (Al Jazeera)
Paraguay prosecutor will seek charges against embattled president after bank collapse (PBS News)
Paraguay Congress rejects President Pena's resignation after bank collapse (Al Jazeera)

chunks.text: On November 5, 2026, the president of Paraguay, a country in South America, said in a video he was {{stepping down}}. Days earlier, a fast-growing online bank {{went under}}, and millions of people were {{cut off}} from their [[savings]]. Minutes after his video, the [[lower house]] of Congress voted 78 to 0 to [[impeach]] him. That means the lower house formally charged him with [[wrongdoing]], so the Senate could hold a trial and remove him.

verbs.wrong: To give a speech to the nation
verbs.why: Many coaches step down after a bad season. Our principal steps down when the school year ends. Paraguay's president said in a video that he was stepping down.

verbs.correct: To fail and close as a business
verbs.wrong: To change its name and logo
verbs.why: Many small shops go under in their first year. A restaurant goes under when it has too few customers. Days earlier, a fast-growing online bank went under.

verbs.correct: To stop someone from using something
verbs.wrong: To send someone a warning letter
verbs.why: The school cuts students off from the Wi-Fi at night. The phone company cuts you off if you never pay the bill. Millions of people were cut off from their savings.

chunks.text: About 3 million people, around 60 percent of adults, had {{signed up}} as customers. The government's central bank {{took over}} the failing bank. Officials said the bank was [[insolvent]], meaning it could not cover its losses. Customers' [[deposits]], their money in the bank, were frozen. The bank's app and cards {{shut down}}, and [[anxious]] customers {{lined up}} outside closed [[branches]].

verbs.correct: To join as a member or customer
verbs.wrong: To earn cash back on groceries
verbs.why: Thousands of students sign up for the free class. My mom signs up for every store's rewards card. About 3 million people signed up as customers of the bank.
The city takes over a building when the owner stops paying taxes. A new company takes over the store in January. In early November, the central bank took over the failing bank.
My laptop shuts down when the battery is empty. The trains shut down during big snowstorms. The bank's app and cards shut down.

verbs.correct: To wait in a row with other people
verbs.why: Fans line up early for concert tickets. Shoppers line up outside the store on Black Friday. Anxious customers lined up outside the bank's closed branches.

chunks.text: Until early 2025, the president owned [[shares]] in the group that owned the bank. The bank held about 800 million dollars of government money, including [[pension]] funds. Lawmakers accused him of a [[conflict of interest]]. He apologized but says he did nothing wrong. His own Colorado Party, led by a former president who was his [[mentor]], {{turned against}} him. A new law says a government fund must {{pay back}} customers within five [[business days]], up to about 36,000 dollars each.

verbs.why: Fans turn against a team when it keeps losing. Voters often turn against a leader when prices rise. The president's own Colorado Party turned against him.

verbs.correct: To return money that is owed
verbs.wrong: To charge a fee for a service
verbs.why: My sister pays me back every time I lend her money. Most people pay back their car loans in five years. A government fund must pay back customers within five business days.

chunks.text: Congress did not accept his resignation. Resigning could have made him a senator for life, protected from [[prosecution]]. A [[joint session]] of both houses ended without a vote after lawmakers from his party {{walked out}}. The Senate {{went ahead with}} the trial on November 6. He did not {{show up}} and sent his lawyers instead. Senators voted 44 to 0 to remove him, and the vice president took his place. Prosecutors placed him under house arrest. Three [[criminal investigations]] will {{look into}} the bank's failure.

verbs.correct: To leave a meeting before it ends
verbs.wrong: To arrive late to a meeting
verbs.why: Some workers walk out when the boss starts shouting. A few parents walk out of the school meeting in protest. The session ended after lawmakers from his party walked out.
The team goes ahead with the game even in light rain. We go ahead with the party when only half the guests can come. The Senate went ahead with the trial on November 6.

verbs.correct: To appear where you are expected
verbs.why: My brother always shows up late for dinner. Everyone shows up for the free pizza. The president did not show up at the Senate and sent his lawyers instead.

verbs.correct: To study something to find the facts
verbs.wrong: To make a new law about something
verbs.why: The school looks into every complaint from parents. Police look into the cause of every fire. Three criminal investigations will look into the bank's failure.

mainIdea.s: Paraguay's leader tried to resign after a fast-growing online bank failed, freezing millions of people's savings. Congress refused, and the Senate then voted to remove him from office.
mainIdea.why: The president said he was stepping down, but Congress did not accept it. The Senate went ahead with the trial and voted to remove him.

mainIdea.s: A South American president offered to quit after a popular bank collapsed. His own party kept defending him, so only opposition lawmakers in the lower house voted to impeach him.
mainIdea.why: Close, but his own Colorado Party turned against him. The lower house voted 78 to 0 to impeach him.

mainIdea.s: Paraguay's central bank plans to open its own phone app so that people can save money more easily. Officials hope low fees and grocery rewards will attract millions of new customers.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a bank that went under and froze people's savings. The president tried to step down, and the Senate removed him from office.

tf.s: Paraguay's president, Santiago Peña, said he was stepping down.
tf.why: He said this in a video on November 5, days after an online bank failed.

tf.s: Congress quickly accepted the president's resignation.
tf.why: Congress did not accept it. A joint session ended without a vote after lawmakers from his party walked out.

tf.s: Millions of people were cut off from their savings.
tf.why: The bank was insolvent, so customers' deposits were frozen and its app and cards stopped working.

tf.s: The president's own party kept supporting him during the crisis.
tf.why: His own Colorado Party turned against him, and even his mentor, a former president, supported impeachment.

tf.s: The central bank took over the bank because it did not have enough money.
tf.why: Officials said the bank was insolvent, meaning it could not cover its losses.

tf.s: Peña admits that he broke the law to help the bank.
tf.why: He denies any wrongdoing. He did not show up at the Senate and sent his lawyers to defend him instead.

lines.text: Did you see that Paraguay's president, Santiago Peña, tried to {{step down}}?
I saw something about a bank. What happened?
A big online bank {{went under}}. About 3 million people had {{signed up}} as customers.
In a country that small? That's a lot of people.
It is. When the central bank {{took over}}, the app and cards {{shut down}}.
So people were {{cut off}} from their own money? That's a saver's [[worst nightmare]].
Pretty much. People {{lined up}} outside closed branches.
Sounds like the bank was a [[house of cards]]. Why is he [[in hot water]]?
He owned shares in the bank's parent group until early 2025. He denies any wrongdoing, though.
He apologized. For a lot of people, it's [[too little, too late]].
And his own party {{turned against}} him?
Yes. Congress didn't even accept his resignation. The Senate {{went ahead with}} impeachment.
Did he {{show up}} for the trial?
No, he sent his lawyers. The Senate removed him, and he's under house arrest now. Prosecutors are also going to {{look into}} the bank's failure.
And the customers? Will anyone {{pay them back}}?
A government fund is supposed to repay most of them. But a lot still [[hangs in the balance]].
